source: Lampinen, Dasgupta, Chan et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks (PNAS Nexus; arXiv v4 of Dasgupta et al. 2022)
finding: Models (Chinchilla, PaLM 2-M/L, Flan-PaLM 2, GPT-3.5-instruct) show the same content effects as people on three tasks: natural language inference (small effect), syllogism validity (large belief effect) and the Wason task (realistic rules easier than arbitrary). Models often beat humans in accuracy and in size of the content effect.
numbers: Human data: 625 UK participants first, then 360 more for Wason (one question per task each). NLI: no significant content effect on accuracy in humans or any model (all p>0.2), but item-level human-model accuracy correlation t(832)=3.49. Wason: significant realistic advantage in humans, Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L, GPT-3.5 (z>2.2, p<0.03); marginal in PaLM 2-M and Flan-PaLM 2 (p about 0.08). New stimuli written to avoid contamination: 12 realistic, 12 arbitrary, 12 nonsense Wason rules plus shuffled and violate controls. Exact accuracies are only in figures, not in text.
quote: humans reason more reliably when the semantic content of a problem supports the correct logical inferences
limits: Models scored by prior-corrected log-probability over fixed answer options, not free generation. Human Wason accuracy was near chance overall; only the slowest 15% (over 80 s) were above chance, and only on realistic rules. Instruction-tuned and base models behaved alike.
agent_relevance: Content effects are a default property of the base model, so our scaffold must assume them and not hope they are absent. Detecting that a problem has a belief-laden surface is the trigger for stripping it (S1 input hygiene).

source: Lampinen et al. (2024) same paper, robustness and prompt analyses (Appx B.2, Discussion)
finding: Plain prompts do not remove content effects. A few NLI examples take Chinchilla from content-biased to near ceiling, and a simple instruction prompt cuts bias a lot. But 5-shot examples on syllogisms only weaken the effect slightly, and on Wason they make it bigger (realistic examples help realistic probes most).
numbers: Chinchilla only for few-shot (5-shot, examples from distinct clusters). Raw-likelihood scoring with an instruction prompt: several models answer 'valid' to everything on syllogisms; removing the instruction reduces that bias and shows stronger content effects. Without prior correction PaLM 2-L scores over 75% in every Wason condition including arbitrary and nonsense.
limits: Few-shot test was Chinchilla only, for computational reasons. Scoring method changes absolute accuracy a lot, so absolute numbers are fragile; direction of content effect is stable.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on few-shot realistic examples to fix abstract problems: they can widen the gap. Prefer a form-only restatement over more examples. Scoring or answer-format choices can swamp the effect we want to measure, so our harness must fix them.

source: Wu, Qiu, Ross, Akyurek, Chen, Wang, Kim, Andreas, Kim (2024) Reasoning or Reciting? Exploring the Capabilities and Limitations of Language Models Through Counterfactual Tasks (NAACL 2024)
finding: On 11 task families (arithmetic in other bases, code with 1-based indexing, chess with swapped pieces, FOLIO logic with false premises, spatial reasoning, music etc.) GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude and PaLM-2 are above chance on counterfactual versions but drop substantially and consistently versus default versions. A comprehension check shows the models understand the new rules, so the drop is not just misreading.
numbers: 0-shot prompting. Table 18 as read: GPT-4 two-digit addition without CoT, 1000 items: base 10 = 100.0%, base 9 = 23.4%, base 11 = 38.4%, base 16 = 63.0%; with 0-shot CoT base 9 = 38.6%; counterfactual comprehension check (200 items) about 90-100%. Gap shrinks with up to 16 few-shot CoT examples but stays large for bases 9, 11, 16 and plateaus.
quote: performance substantially and consistently degrades compared to the default conditions
limits: Counterfactual worlds are partly confounded with difficulty and commonness (bases 9 and 11 are rarer than 10 and 16). Table text was reconstructed from a flattened PDF; check against the paper before quoting a single cell.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that models lean on familiar surface instances of a task. The scaffold should test any answer on a counterfactual or relabelled copy (fits G3: pass on something the answer was not fitted to).

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or Reciting?, logic task (FOLIO with common-sense-violating premises)
finding: When the premises of FOLIO items are rewritten to be false in the real world, and the model is told to use no common sense, GPT-4 still loses about 20 points. A regression on all 1,204 FOLIO items shows correctness rises with the share of premises the model itself believes true.
numbers: Only 81 FOLIO items were hand-rewritten (items where all premises and conclusion truth matched GPT-4 belief); a second author checked the rewrite. GPT-4 as read from Table 23: default 93.8 vs counterfactual 74.1 without CoT; 98.8 vs 82.7 with 0-shot CoT. Other models also lower on counterfactual (rows hard to align in the flattened table).
limits: N=81 is small; no confidence intervals in the table. Other-model cells could not be assigned with confidence.
agent_relevance: Telling the model 'use no common sense' is not enough. A real fix must remove the content or hand the logic to a checker.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or Reciting?, prompting analyses (Sec 5.4-5.5)
finding: 0-shot chain of thought usually helps but can hurt: it lowers PaLM-2 base-10 and base-16 addition and GPT chord-playing in the default tuning. The authors guess overthinking on easy items or memorised answers. Few-shot CoT with up to 16 demos does not close the default-counterfactual gap.
numbers: Few-shot CoT up to 16 samples on arithmetic; gap remains for bases 9, 11, 16; improvement plateaus near 16-shot.
limits: Arithmetic only for the few-shot test. Authors state the reasons for CoT harm are hypotheses.
agent_relevance: Supports G1 (doubt or extra thinking only on a signal): forced step-by-step can lower accuracy on easy default cases.

source: Tang, Zheng, Li, Meng, Zhu, Liang, Zhang (2023) Large Language Models are In-Context Semantic Reasoners rather than Symbolic Reasoners
finding: Replace meaningful words with symbols (r1, r2, e4...) or with counter-commonsense relations, and ChatGPT and GPT-4 deduce and induce much worse. Real semantics let the model use stored knowledge as a shortcut. Counter-commonsense rules are harder than meaningless symbols.
numbers: Symbolic Tree, deduction, Few-Shot-CoT (Table 4), ChatGPT / GPT-4: Semantics 71.8 / 90.0; Symbols 53.7 / 67.6; remove-rules-and-facts 70.1 / 90.4; Counter-commonsense 48.9 / 73.4. Induction (zero-shot CoT): Semantics 25.0 / 53.6; Symbols 7.14 / 21.4; Counter-CS 7.14 / 17.8. Removing the in-context rules and facts barely hurt deduction, so the model was using memory, not the given premises.
quote: LLMs perform significantly better when semantics are consistent with commonsense but struggle to solve symbolic or counter-commonsense reasoning tasks
limits: Preprint, under review at the time. Tree datasets are relations like family ties, so the common-sense prior is strong. A logic-based solver baseline got 100% on deduction, so symbols are not hard per se.
agent_relevance: Key warning for abstraction: stripping content to symbols can lower accuracy for a pure LLM. Stripping only pays if a program does the reasoning on the stripped form, not the LLM.

source: Tang et al. (2023) in-context semantic reasoners, ProofWriter and CoT results
finding: On ProofWriter (rules unrelated to common sense) symbols and odd semantics perform about the same zero-shot, but with CoT the odd-semantics version is worse and CoT is worse than zero-shot. Step-by-step reasoning seems to amplify the pull of odd meanings ('the squirrel needs the dog') and increases 'cannot be determined' answers.
numbers: ChatGPT zero-shot depth-1 about 69% in both settings, falling to about 53-60% at depth 5; CoT variants lower. Table rows were garbled in text extraction, so only the pattern is reliable.
limits: One model on this dataset; exact cells uncertain.
agent_relevance: CoT is not a safe default when content conflicts with the rule set; another reason to check by code (G2, G5).

source: Saparov and He (2023) Language Models Are Greedy Reasoners: A Systematic Formal Analysis of Chain-of-Thought (ICLR 2023)
finding: PrOntoQA tests the same proof trees with fictional, true and false ontologies. GPT-3 (text-davinci-002) does about as well on fictional and false ontologies, much better on true ones, and with a true ontology it does not lose accuracy from 3 to 5 hops because it can skip hops with stored knowledge. Individual proof steps are mostly valid; the weakness is choosing which step to take (planning).
numbers: 400 examples per condition, 48 experiments, Wilson 95% CI; only the largest model (text-davinci-002) beat chance. Exact accuracies are in figures.
quote: Evidently, the model's reasoning is heavily reliant on real-world knowledge
limits: Older model (2022). Single model for the main results.
agent_relevance: Supports using fictional renamings to measure true reasoning, and shows content helps when consistent with the logic (skip-hop) and does not help when false.

source: Eisape, Tessler, Dasgupta, Sha, van Steenkiste, Linzen (2024) A Systematic Comparison of Syllogistic Reasoning in Humans and Language Models (NAACL 2024)
finding: PaLM 2 models are more logical than people on syllogisms and larger is better, but even the best get only about 75%. Errors are systematic: order of variables (A-C vs C-A) matters, they draw confident wrong conclusions on classic fallacy forms, and with chain of thought they almost never say 'nothing follows'. A binary 'does this follow?' format raises accuracy on 'nothing follows' items a lot.
numbers: Human data from Ragni et al. 2019: 139 participants, human mean accuracy about 50%. Syllogism forms filled with 30 content triples; 30 samples at temperature 0.5, max 75 tokens, per item. Accuracy near 0% on 'nothing follows' under the zero-shot CoT generative method; binary discrimination 'markedly higher' on those items (Fig 13). Llama 2 family replicates the trends.
quote: language models often mimic the human biases included in their training data, but are able to overcome them in some cases
limits: Content here is mild (neutral words), so belief effects are small by design; the study is mainly about form effects.
agent_relevance: Ask the question as a binary validity check, not as 'what follows'. For categorical syllogisms, force the 'nothing follows' option and score all candidate conclusions in code.

source: Eisape et al. (2024) mReasoner comparison (Sec 5)
finding: The authors fit a cognitive model, mReasoner (mental-model theory), with four parameters: LEN (number of entities built), BROAD (how wide a set of individuals is sampled), SYSTEM2 (chance of searching for a counterexample) and WEAKEN (chance of weakening a too-strong conclusion). It builds a small model, draws a quick conclusion, then maybe looks for counterexamples. They use it to explain which human-like errors the LMs share.
numbers: Parameter grid: LEN 2.0-4.5, BROAD 0-0.9, SYSTEM2 0-0.9, WEAKEN 0-0.9 (Table 3).
limits: Only the description in this paper was read, not the original mReasoner paper (Khemlani and Johnson-Laird 2022).
agent_relevance: A tested cognitive program with the shape we want: quick answer, then counterexample search only when triggered. The counterexample search is an operator we can run in code.

source: Ando, Morishita, Abe, Mineshima, Okada (2023) Evaluating Large Language Models with NeuBAROCO: Syllogistic Reasoning Ability and Human-like Biases
finding: On 375 English/Japanese syllogism items labelled for belief bias, conversion errors and atmosphere effects, GPT-3.5, RoBERTa and BART are worst on belief-inconsistent items, and do very badly where conversion or atmosphere would give a wrong answer.
numbers: GPT-3.5 English: overall 51.73; symbol items 61.05; belief-consistent 56.89; belief-inconsistent 31.37; conversion-trap items 25.71; atmosphere-trap items 39.42. RoBERTa 34.67 overall, 22.55 inconsistent, 0.0 on conversion and atmosphere. BART overall 35.20, 15.69 inconsistent.
limits: Old models. Abstract-symbol items did not beat consistent items by much for GPT-3.5 (61 vs 57), so 'abstraction helps' is weak here. No human data run in this paper.
agent_relevance: Belief-inconsistent items are the hard test for any content-stripping step. We should build our own eval with matched consistent / inconsistent / symbol triples.

source: Ozeki, Ando, Morishita, Abe, Mineshima, Okada (2024) Exploring Reasoning Biases in LLMs Through Syllogism: Insights from the NeuBAROCO Dataset (Findings ACL 2024)
finding: GPT-4 is the best model by far and is still worst on belief-incongruent, conversion and atmosphere items and on 'neutral' items (neither follows nor contradicts). A prompt that first translates the syllogism into predicate logic or set theory, then explains, translates almost perfectly but raises final accuracy only a little. So the limit is the reasoning step, not the reading.
numbers: 790 NLI items, 80 multiple-choice, 90 translate-and-explain. NLI English GPT-4: zero-shot 71.77 overall, few-shot 77.47; few-shot neutral label 61.78 (zero-shot 50.29); congruent 82.92 vs incongruent 67.23 (few-shot; zero-shot 76.24 vs 61.76); conversion traps 50.00, atmosphere traps 59.41. GPT-3.5 49.75 zero-shot. Translate-and-explain, GPT-4 English: explanation only 77.78; with predicate-logic translation final answer 83.33 (translation correct 96.67%, 87/90); with set-theory translation 80.00 (translation correct 92.22%). GPT-3.5: 58.89 explanation only, 52.22 and 54.44 with translations (flat or worse). Japanese GPT-4: 70.00 to 75.56 / 74.44.
limits: Few-shot and zero-shot rows are interleaved in the flattened table; I assigned them by row order. Small N (90) for the translate test. GPT-3.5 gains nothing from translation.
agent_relevance: Formalisation by the model alone gives about +5 points for the strongest model and nothing for a weaker one. The gain should come from a solver or code doing the inference after translation.

source: Macmillan-Scott and Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and Cognitive Biases in Large Language Models (arXiv 2402.09193)
finding: Seven models on twelve classic tasks including the abstract Wason task and a facilitated (post-office) Wason: models are irrational, but mostly in non-human ways, and highly inconsistent across ten runs. The facilitated Wason version did not help the way it helps people; only the AIDS task showed the human easier-version pattern among four task pairs.
numbers: Each task prompted 10 times, zero-shot. GPT-4 gave the correct answer with correct reasoning in 69.2% of cases, Claude 2 in 55.0%; Llama 2 7B was wrong in 77.5% of cases. Most wrong answers showed illogical reasoning, not a known human bias. One Bard Wason answer reasoned correctly (turn letters 3 and 4) but stated only letter 4.
quote: incorrect responses were generally not human-like
limits: Per-task Wason numbers are in figures only. Models include now-old versions (Bard, Claude 2, Llama 2). Small prompt set per task.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a human-like content benefit. Check the actual answer against the reasoning by code (G2); reasoning and final answer can disagree.

source: Seals and Shalin (2024) Evaluating the Deductive Competence of Large Language Models (NAACL 2024)
finding: Wason task with matched sets across arbitrary, shuffled and realistic content, social and non-social rules, and four presentation formats, on 7B-class open models (Guanaco, MPT, BLOOM, Falcon) plus others. Realistic rules help vs arbitrary; social rules show an interaction like Cosmides 1989 (switched social contracts lower). But performance stays low, social content helps less than in people, and format changes give odd interactions with content that humans do not show.
numbers: Chance is 1/6 (all two-card choices). Realistic vs shuffled OR 1.30 [1.05-1.62]; social-rule x content interaction OR 1.59 [1.26-2.02]; switched social rules lower than standard. LLMs solve social-rule problems about 30% of the time vs about 70% reported for humans. No effect of which LLM. Models pick the antecedent card less often than humans do, and this varies by condition.
quote: social content does not benefit LLM performance as might be expected based on training corpus content
limits: Small 2023 open models only; scored with domain-conditional PMI. The authors cite Dasgupta v1 as reporting Chinchilla about 50% on realistic and chance on arbitrary zero-shot.
agent_relevance: Small models show a weak social-contract signal. A frontier model in an agent loop may differ (see c15). Present rules in canonical form before judging.

source: Abe, Ozeki, Ando, Morishita, Mineshima, Okada (2026) Evaluation of Deontic Conditional Reasoning in LLMs: The Case of Wason's Selection Task (EACL 2026 short)
finding: With a new dataset that marks deontic versus descriptive rules, all nine tested models do better on deontic rules in every prompt type. Errors on deontic rules look like matching bias (picking the cards that name words in the rule) more than confirmation bias. Reasoning-trained models almost solve the deontic version, yet still miss some descriptive ones.
numbers: 160 problems: 80 deontic, 80 descriptive, 20 per polarity pattern (Pos-Pos, Pos-Neg, Neg-Pos, Neg-Neg). Deontic accuracy, zero-shot (gain over descriptive in points): gpt-oss-20b 67.5 (+27.5), gpt-oss-120b 100.0 (+30), qwen3-14b 97.5 (+45), qwen3-32b 98.8 (+38.8), gemma3-4b 17.5 (+5), gemma3-12b 58.8 (+30.1), gemma3-27b 77.5 (+38.7), llama-3.3-70b 62.5 (+10), olmo-2-32b 36.2 (+15). CoT: llama-3.3-70b 83.8 (+38.8), olmo 57.5. Few-shot: gpt-oss-20b 91.2 (+41.2). Deontic advantage ranged 5.0 to 41.2 points. Temperature 0; reasoning models given 6,000-11,000 tokens.
limits: Open-weight models only, no GPT-4 or Claude. Descriptive rules are a different wording, not necessarily the abstract letter-number card. Some matching-bias choices are also logically right (FC card). Few problems per cell (20).
agent_relevance: Best direct machine evidence for deontic-vs-indicative effects. Recasting an indicative rule as an explicit obligation or permission ('must / may') before looking for violations is a cheap operator, with large gains for small models.

source: Bertolazzi, Gatt, Bernardi (2024) A Systematic Analysis of Large Language Models as Soft Reasoners: The Case of Syllogistic Inferences (EMNLP 2024)
finding: Compares zero-shot CoT, in-context learning (ICL) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on Pythia and LLaMA with believable and unbelievable syllogisms. Pre-trained models show content effects and almost never say 'nothing follows'. ICL raises accuracy on valid forms but makes answers more contradictory. Only SFT mitigates most biases and fixes 'nothing follows'. The authors link the SFT effect to training on pseudo-words and varied content.
numbers: LLaMA-3 8B zero-shot CoT: overall 30.31; valid-believable 70.74 vs valid-unbelievable 52.59. LLaMA-3 8B instruct 50.00 overall. Human accuracy on the same forms about 44.6% valid, 41.0% invalid. After SFT LLaMA-3 8B reaches about 96% overall (about 97% invalid, 99% valid, as read) with content effect 4.68%. ICL raises contradictory answers; Pythia after SFT still gave 73.91% contradictory answers. Three seeds per cell.
quote: only the latter mitigates most reasoning biases without harming model consistency
limits: Training is outside our scheme (we do not train). Small open models. Table cells hard to align in extracted text, so some column assignments are uncertain.
agent_relevance: Our no-training constraint rules SFT out. The finding that nonsense-word variety teaches form-only logic suggests running each check on several renamed copies and comparing in code.

source: Bertolazzi, Pezzelle, Bernardi (2026) How Language Models Conflate Logical Validity with Plausibility: A Representational Analysis of Content Effects (v3, April 2026)
finding: Inside the model, 'valid' and 'plausible' are two linear directions that are strongly aligned, so adding the plausibility direction flips validity judgements and vice versa. The more aligned they are in a model, the bigger its behavioural content effect. A debiasing vector that separates them cuts content effect. Chain-of-thought prompts also reduce content effect compared to zero-shot.
numbers: Dataset of syllogisms covering all 64 forms with ten term triples, 70-30 split. Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct: content effect (CE) 0.348 zero-shot; steering at scale 1.5 raised accuracy 81.62 to 82.21 and cut CE to 0.072. Qwen3-14B: accuracy 86.54 to 96.70, CE 0.213 to 0.043. Regression: zero-shot prompts add CE vs CoT (coef 0.188, p<0.001). Qwen3 zero-shot accuracies 80.61 (4B) to 90.91 (32B).
limits: Needs hidden-state access and a layer choice; not usable through an API. Small dataset. Control tasks (harmful, hypernym) used to show specificity.
agent_relevance: Explains why 'ignore plausibility' prompts fail: the model has no clean separate signal. For an API-only agent, the practical equivalent is to make plausibility irrelevant by removing it from the input.

source: Valentino et al. (2026) Mitigating Content Effects on Reasoning in Language Models Through Fine-Grained Activation Steering (v3, April 2026)
finding: Static activation steering can reduce content bias in some models, but not all. A conditional method (K-CAST, steers only when a nearest-neighbour check says so) gives up to 15 points absolute gain in formal-reasoning accuracy on a model that did not respond to static steering. It is robust to prompt variations, with small side effects on multilingual modelling and partial transfer to other tasks.
numbers: Over 16k syllogistic arguments instantiated from abstract schemes. Llama 3.2 3B baseline accuracy 77.79 with CE 17.50. Models include Llama 3.2 3B and Qwen 2.5 7B. Up to about +15 points absolute with K-CAST.
quote: a static approach is insufficient to debias all the tested models
limits: White-box only, small open models. Conditional steering needs a training set for the kNN.
agent_relevance: Signal-triggered intervention beats always-on intervention, the same principle as G1.

source: Kim, Valentino, Freitas (2025) Reasoning Circuits in Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Syllogistic Inference (Findings ACL 2025; arXiv 2408.08590)
finding: Circuit discovery shows a small circuit that suppresses the middle term to infer the conclusion on abstract (symbolic) syllogisms, working across model sizes. On belief-consistent data the circuit is sufficient; on belief-inconsistent data recovery fails, pointing to extra attention heads that inject world knowledge.
numbers: Qualitative: circuit sufficiency holds on belief-consistent non-symbolic data and fails on belief-inconsistent data. No single accuracy figure used.
limits: Mechanistic study on small open models; figures only partly readable in text extraction.
agent_relevance: Supports a two-route view: a form route that works on symbols plus a content route that can override it. Keeping content out of the input keeps the model on the form route.

source: Poddar, Sahoo, Ghosh (2025) Understanding Syllogistic Reasoning in LLMs from Formal and Natural Language Perspectives (v3 Dec 2025)
finding: 14 models, four prompt strategies, three temperatures on 160 syllogisms (40 base items times natural, nonsense (X), order-switched (O), and both). Top models are near-perfect on formal validity and give the same answer on natural and nonsense versions (consistency about 99%), yet 12 of 14 show positive belief bias. Formal accuracy (81.7% mean) far exceeds accuracy at judging believability (56.2%).
numbers: 26,880 model-instance evaluations. Syntax accuracy: Gemini 2.5 Flash 99.6, GPT-OSS-20B and Gemini 2.5 Pro about 99.5, Kimi-K2 99.3, DeepSeek V3.1 99.0 ... Llama 3.2 1B 51.9. Bimodal: six models above 95, five below 70. Dataset: 76 valid (47.5%), 84 invalid, 82 congruent (51.2%), 78 incongruent. Natural-vs-nonsense consistency 99.2 for Gemini 2.5 Flash. Qwen3-Next Thinking: precision 99.2 but recall 42.8 (calls most syllogisms invalid).
limits: Preprint; very small dataset. Belief bias defined as accuracy gap congruent minus incongruent; believability labels are noisy (only 23.8% believable).
agent_relevance: For top models nonsense-word renaming is nearly lossless, so a nonsense-renaming operator is safe on strong models; a weak model needs a solver.

source: Nguyen, Tachibana, Liu, Liu, Noe, Takeda, Kurohashi (2026) BIS Reasoning 1.0: The First Large-Scale Japanese Benchmark for Belief-Inconsistent Syllogistic Reasoning (v5, March 2026)
finding: 5,000 valid but belief-inconsistent Japanese syllogisms, zero-shot. Reasoning-trained models are near ceiling; GPT-4o is about 80%; Claude 3 models are far below chance on this set despite fair scores on NeuBAROCO. Performance depends heavily on how much hidden reasoning the model is allowed.
numbers: GPT-5-mini 99.7%, Qwen3-32B above 99%, GPT-5-nano 98.8% at medium effort but 69.2% at minimum effort, GPT-4o 79.54% (94.01% on NeuBAROCO), Claude-3-sonnet 20.34% and Claude-3-opus 7.18% (78.44% and 61.07% on NeuBAROCO), llm-jp-3.1-13b-instruct4 84.66%. N=5,000 per model.
quote: performance is sensitive to prompt design and inference-time reasoning effort
limits: Japanese language, yes/no format; a score of 7% on a binary task implies systematic wrong answers or format failures, which the paper does not fully separate. Old Claude 3 models only.
agent_relevance: Thinking budget is a large lever on belief bias. The scaffold should spend compute on the form check, not on extra general thinking.

source: Nguyen et al. (2026) BIS Reasoning 1.0, prompt analysis on 100 GPT-4o failures (Sec 4.3)
finding: Re-asking 100 items GPT-4o got wrong with different prompts shows plain, casual and simple prompts rescue almost nothing, while an explicit step-by-step prompt rescues most and a prompt saying 'strict logic, beliefs may conflict' rescues many. Politeness gives a moderate gain.
numbers: Recovery on the 100 failed items: CoT prompt 87%; logic-focus prompt that names possible belief conflict about 76%; polite 65%; casual 3%; basic 5%. English prompts repeated the pattern.
limits: Selected on failure (regression to the mean may inflate recovery); one model; N=100. Matching 76% to the logic-focus prompt rests on reading order in the text and should be double-checked.
agent_relevance: A prompt that names the conflict explicitly plus step-by-step beats a generic 'be logical'. Cheap to test as an S1 hygiene note, but keep G7 (equal tokens vs plain).

source: Akinfaderin and Diallo (2026) FregeLogic at SemEval-2026 Task 11: A Hybrid Neuro-Symbolic Architecture for Content-Robust Syllogistic Validity Prediction
finding: An agent-style loop: five LLM classifiers (Llama 4 Maverick and Scout, Qwen3-32B with different prompts) vote; only when the vote is narrow does a Z3 solver, fed a formalisation of the syllogism, act as tiebreaker. Close votes coincide with content-biased errors. The tiebreaker cuts content effect 16% and adds 0.9 points.
numbers: N=960 syllogisms, nested 5-fold CV, balanced over valid/invalid x believable/unbelievable. Pure ensemble 93.4% accuracy, CE 3.39, combined score 39.12. Tiebreaker 94.3%, CE 2.85, score 41.88 (score = Acc/(1+ln(1+CE))). Narrow-vote splits were 7.9% of cases (76 of 960). Invalid-believable accuracy 90.2 to 94.5. Structured-output extraction cut Z3 failure from 22% to near zero.
limits: Shared-task system paper; gain is small in absolute terms. Same 960 items used for tuning folds. Task score favours low CE.
agent_relevance: Close fit to our design: disagreement triggers a code check (G1, G4). Direct template for a formalise-then-verify operator.

source: Akinfaderin and Diallo (2026) FregeLogic, Z3-only baseline and invalidity bias (Sec 5.4)
finding: Formalising to logic does not by itself remove content problems. Z3 alone, fed LLM-extracted formulas, got only 74.7% accuracy because extraction errors on valid syllogisms break the proof, so it calls most valid ones invalid. The solver is correct; the translation step is the weak part.
numbers: Z3-only: accuracy 74.7%, CE 26.28; accuracy on invalid syllogisms 97.6% (IB 98.0, IU 97.2) but valid only 52.2% (VB 50.5, VU 53.9). On narrow 3-2 splits Z3 was right only 48.6% of the time on valid items. Authors tried Z3 veto (score 17.18), weighted, and confidence-based fusions; all worse than tiebreaker.
limits: One task format (categorical syllogisms with Aristotelian existence axioms). Prompts and encoding choices matter.
agent_relevance: A formaliser has its own failure direction. Treat 'solver says not entailed' as weak evidence, never as proof (G3), and check the translation with a held-out paraphrase.

source: Pan, Albalak, Wang, Wang (2023) Logic-LM: Empowering Large Language Models with Symbolic Solvers for Faithful Logical Reasoning (Findings EMNLP 2023)
finding: The LLM translates the problem into a symbolic form, a deterministic solver (Prover9, Z3, python-constraint, pyke) infers, and a self-refinement loop feeds solver error messages back to fix the formalisation. Outperforms standard prompting and CoT on average across five logic datasets.
numbers: Accuracy (Standard / CoT / Logic-LM). GPT-4: PrOntoQA 77.40/98.79/83.20; ProofWriter 52.67/68.11/79.66; FOLIO 69.11/70.58/78.92; LogicalDeduction 71.33/75.25/87.63; AR-LSAT 33.33/35.06/43.04. ChatGPT: ProofWriter 35.50/49.17/58.33; FOLIO 45.09/57.35/62.74. Average gain with GPT-3.5: +39.2 over standard and +18.4 over CoT; with GPT-4 +24.98 over standard and +10.44 over CoT. Self-refinement raised executable rate by 5.01 on average.
limits: On PrOntoQA GPT-4 CoT (98.79) beat Logic-LM (83.20). Executable rate for GPT-4 on FOLIO only 79.9% and AR-LSAT 32.6%; failures fall back to CoT. Real-world problems are hard to formalise.
agent_relevance: Matches our operator set: formalise, run solver, repair from the solver's real error output (G2). Keep fallback to plain answer (G6).

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM, depth analysis
finding: The solver advantage grows with reasoning depth because translation difficulty stays constant while chain length grows. CoT and standard prompting drop sharply with depth.
numbers: Logic-LM minus CoT on ProofWriter by depth (GPT-4): +7.1 (depth 0), +5.0 (1), +12.7 (2), +20.0 (4), +39.4 (5).
limits: Synthetic ProofWriter has low language variety. The advantage is small or reversed on easy data (PrOntoQA).
agent_relevance: Use the formalise-and-solve route when the problem has several inference steps or content conflict; for one-step items the plain route is as good (G7).

source: Olausson, Gu, Lipkin, Zhang, Solar-Lezama, Tenenbaum, Levy (2023) LINC: A Neurosymbolic Approach for Logical Reasoning by Combining Language Models with First-Order Logic Provers (EMNLP 2023)
finding: LLM as semantic parser into first-order logic, Prover9 does the deduction, K=10 formalisations are majority-voted. Large gain on ProofWriter for all models and on FOLIO for the smaller ones; for GPT-4 on FOLIO LINC does not beat CoT. LINC and CoT make very different mistakes.
numbers: FOLIO 182 items; ProofWriter balanced subset. Bootstrapped 10-way means. FOLIO: StarCoder+ LINC 56.0 vs best baseline 41.8; GPT-3.5 LINC 62.6 vs 54.9; GPT-4 LINC 72.5 vs CoT 75.3. ProofWriter: GPT-3.5 LINC 96.4%, GPT-4 LINC 98.3%, GPT-4 CoT about 72% (abstract: +26 points). Syntax-error rate in FOL: 38% StarCoder+, 24% GPT-3.5, 13% GPT-4. Failure types: FOL misses implicit facts (e.g. Person(Harry)), loses information in the chosen representation (one symbol NaziGermanPolitician), syntax mistakes.
limits: Small test sets. Gains are largest on synthetic ProofWriter. Real-text FOLIO needs implicit world knowledge, which a content-stripped formal route loses.
agent_relevance: Formalisation strips content but also drops needed background facts. The scaffold should allow a content-aware route for real-world items, with agreement between routes as a check.

source: Ye, Chen, Dillig, Durrett (2023) SatLM: Satisfiability-Aided Language Models Using Declarative Prompting (NeurIPS 2023)
finding: Ask the LLM for a declarative specification (constraints) instead of a step-by-step program, and let a SAT/SMT solver search. Beats program-aided models on 8 datasets, especially where search and planning are needed.
numbers: GSM-SYS (hard subset needing equation systems): 69.4% greedy and 80.9% with self-consistency, over 20 points above program-aided LM and CoT. GSM 84.8% with self-consistency. LSAT new state of the art 37.4 (from 30.9). BoardgameQA 80.7 (from 73.9). Regex 44.0 vs 37.1 for the imperative program.
limits: Code-davinci / gpt-3.5 era numbers. Not a content-effect study; it is the closest method showing a declarative form lowers translation error.
agent_relevance: Declarative (what is true) stays closer to the text than procedural (how to compute), so there is less room for content to creep in during translation.

source: Lyu, Havaldar, Stein, Zhang, Rao, Wong, Apidianaki, Callison-Burch (2023) Faithful Chain-of-Thought Reasoning (IJCNLP-AACL 2023)
finding: Two stages: LLM translates the question into a symbolic reasoning chain (code, logic, or Datalog), a deterministic solver answers. This makes the chain the real cause of the answer. Beats standard CoT on 9 of 10 datasets.
numbers: Relative accuracy gains over CoT: +6.3% math word problems, +3.4% planning, +5.5% multi-hop QA, +21.4% relational inference.
limits: Translation errors are still possible; the guarantee is only that the chain explains the answer.
agent_relevance: Basis for a rule: the reasoning chain shown must be the thing a program executes, not free text.

source: Zheng, Mishra, Chen, Cheng, Chi, Le, Zhou (2024) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in Large Language Models (ICLR 2024)
finding: Abstraction prompting: first ask a higher-level question (what principle or concept applies?), then answer using that principle. Helps in physics, chemistry, time-sensitive QA and multi-hop QA. It is abstraction in the sense of principles, not content-stripping.
numbers: PaLM-2L: MMLU Physics 66.4 to 73.2 (CoT 65.0); MMLU Chemistry 70.9 to 81.8 (CoT 75.3); TimeQA 41.5 with about +27 points; MuSiQue +7. GPT-4: Physics 69.4 to 84.5 (CoT 82.9); Chemistry 80.9 to 85.6 (CoT 85.3). Llama2-70B: Physics 51.9 to 64.8. Error analysis: step-back fixes up to about 40% of base errors and creates at most about 12% new ones. Five runs each.
limits: Gain over CoT for GPT-4 is small (1.6 and 0.3 points). Not tested on belief-conflict logic problems.
agent_relevance: A principle-first step is an abstraction operator with real but modest evidence. For content effects the right abstraction is 'what is the logical form, and which cases could falsify it?'

source: Mirzadeh, Alizadeh, Shahrokhi, Tuzel, Bengio, Farajtabar (2025) GSM-Symbolic: Understanding the Limitations of Mathematical Reasoning in LLMs (ICLR 2025)
finding: Re-instantiating the same GSM8K templates with new names and numbers makes accuracy vary and fall. Changing only names causes noticeable variance; changing numbers causes more. Adding one irrelevant but plausible clause (GSM-NoOp) causes large drops even with eight same-question shots.
numbers: Gap between best and worst of the sampled sets exceeds 12% for Gemma2-9B. NoOp drops: up to 65% for Phi-3-mini; o1-preview -17.5 points; Gemma-7b-it -20.6; Mistral-7b -24.0. Performance falls and variance rises as clauses are added.
limits: Math, not logic. The authors' explanation (pattern matching, not reasoning) is a hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Supports an irrelevance-removal step in S1 and a rename-and-recheck test. A single surplus clause can derail even strong reasoners.

source: Chen, Chi, Wang, Zhou (2024) Premise Order Matters in Reasoning with Large Language Models (ICML 2024)
finding: Shuffling the order of premises (no change to meaning) can cut deductive accuracy by over 30%. Best accuracy comes when premise order matches the order of the proof. The same effect appears in an order-shuffled GSM8K (R-GSM).
numbers: Accuracy drop from permuting premise order up to over 30%; on R-GSM, GPT-4-turbo and PaLM 2-L fall about 20-30% and some other models by more than 40%.
limits: Not content but form of presentation; included because it shows surface form beyond content also matters.
agent_relevance: Put premises into canonical order in code before any model sees them; an easy form-normalisation operator.

source: Saparov, Pang, Padmakumar, Joshi, Kazemi, Kim, He (2023) Testing the General Deductive Reasoning Capacity of LLMs Using OOD Examples (NeurIPS 2023)
finding: Uses fictional concept names throughout to stop pre-training knowledge from helping, over many deduction rules. Models generalise to compositional proofs but struggle with longer proofs and need explicit demos to build hypothetical sub-proofs (proof by cases and by contradiction).
numbers: Four LLMs of different size and training objectives; no single headline accuracy in the abstract.
limits: Read only the abstract, intro and data-construction text, not the results tables.
agent_relevance: Confirms that fictional naming is standard practice for checking form-only reasoning; supports using it as our evaluation control.

source: Oaksford and Chater (1994) A rational analysis of the selection task as optimal data selection (Psychological Review 101)
finding: Older computational model: people pick cards by expected information gain under a rarity assumption (antecedent and consequent are rare), not by falsification. Predicts why content that changes rarity changes choices, with no special social module.
numbers: Not read; cited from memory. No figures claimed here.
limits: Not opened. Known to be contested for deontic rules, where utility rather than information is said to drive choice.
agent_relevance: A rival account to Cosmides and Tooby. A computed expected-information-gain score per case could be one operator for choosing which cases to test.

source: Search note (2026-10-20): no LLM study found of Cosmides-Tooby cheater detection, Cheng-Holyoak schemas, or relevance theory
finding: Across the searches I could run before the web-search quota ran out, no paper tested language models on social-contract or cheater-detection stimuli as such, nor tested pragmatic-reasoning-schema prompts, nor used Sperber's relevance theory in an LLM loop. The closest are c14 (social vs non-social Wason, 7B models) and c15 (deontic vs descriptive, nine models).
numbers: Searches that ran: about 8 targeted queries. The final queries for Cosmides and Tooby and for Cheng and Holyoak could not run (quota).
limits: Absence of evidence from limited searches, not proof. Repeat the two blocked searches later.
agent_relevance: These parts of the subfield are unmeasured for machines, so treat any schema built on them as [D] design choice until we test it.
